reason: Multiple independent sources verify the core scientific discovery, the widespread social hysteria, and the physical reality of the comet tail.
story: In 1910, the return of Halley’s Comet triggered a global panic that science itself accidentally sparked. While tracking the comet, astronomers at Yerkes Observatory used a new tool called a spectrograph to analyze its tail. They discovered cyanogen—a deadly poison gas. When French astronomer Camille Flammarion suggested the gas might "snuff out all life" as Earth passed through the tail, newspapers ignored the scientific caveats about the tail's low density. Hysteria exploded. Families sealed their homes with wet towels, while others bought "comet pills" or gas masks from opportunistic hucksters. Some even held rooftop "comet parties" to toast the apocalypse. On the night of May 18, Earth glided through the tail’s outer streamers. The result? Absolutely nothing. The tail was so rarefied it was effectively a vacuum. Life continued, leaving only the "pill" sellers rich and the sensationalist media looking for their next big scare.
angle: In 1910, the discovery of cyanide gas in Halley's Comet caused a global hysteria where people bought 'comet pills' and sealed their houses to survive a cosmic suffocation that never happened.

claims.claim: Halley's Comet made a predicted return to Earth's vicinity in 1910.
In February 1910, Yerkes Observatory announced the detection of cyanogen gas in the comet's tail.
Cyanogen is a poisonous gas chemically related to cyanide.
Astronomers identified the gas using spectroscopic analysis of the comet's light.
Calculations indicated that Earth would pass directly through the comet's tail on May 18-19, 1910.
French astronomer Camille Flammarion warned that the gas could possibly snuff out all life on Earth.
Newspapers sensationalized the findings, running headlines about mass suffocation and doom.
Working astronomers emphasized that the comet's tail was so diffuse it was essentially a vacuum.
Hucksters sold 'comet pills,' which were often just sugar, to protect against the gas.
Gas masks and mouth inhalers became best-sellers as the comet approached.
Some people used wet towels to seal windows and doors against the perceived poison.
'Comet-protecting umbrellas' were sold as a defense against the comet's effects.
'Comet parties' were held on rooftops to toast the end of the world.
Reports of suicides and heart failures were attributed to the mass hysteria over the comet.
Author Mark Twain died in April 1910, fulfilling his prediction that he would 'go out' with the comet.
Earth passed through the tail with no detected harmful effects or air quality changes.
The Great January Comet of 1910 appeared earlier that year and was brighter than Halley's Comet.
Edmond Halley used Newton's laws to predict the comet's periodic return every 76 years.

disputed: The death of King Edward VII is linked to comet fear only in S5; the script should leave this out as a primary claim.
Specific reports of voodoo rituals in Haiti are unique to S4; attribute to 'some reports' if used.
Specific olfactory reports of burning vegetables or marsh smells are only in S5; attribute to 'some observers' or leave out.
The 'telephonic error' naming the January comet 'Drake's Comet' is only in S1; leave out.

sources.title: On the night of May 18–19, 1910, Earth passed through the tail of Halley’s Comet, three months after astronomers detected the poisonous gas cyanogen within it. Sensational reports helped entrepreneurs sell anti-comet pills, mouth inhalers and even comet insurance—but the tail was so extraordinarily diffuse that no harmful effect was detected.
